title: Spirals and supernovae
caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 1015, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 1015 · constellation Cetus · about 120 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Ranked #19 on ESA/Hubble’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: Symmetrical arms swirl out from a bright central bulge in this face-on Hubble view, like a Catherine wheel firework. This is NGC 1015, a barred spiral galaxy about 118 million light-years from Earth in the constellation Cetus, the Whale.

The galaxy has a fairly large, bright center, smooth and tightly wound arms, and a bar of stars and gas across the middle, much like our own Milky Way. Its arms curl outwards from a pale yellow ring around the bar. Bars appear in roughly two-thirds of all spiral galaxies. Scientists believe they may act as channels, funnelling gas and energy from the outer arms toward the core, where they could feed a central black hole, fuel star birth and build up the bulge.
In 2009, astronomers spotted a Type Ia supernova, SN 2009ig, in this galaxy. It shows up as one of the bright points above and to the right of the galaxy's core.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (1.97 x 2.27 arcminutes) and distance (120 million light years), the frame spans roughly 69,000 × 79,000 light-years. Its light set out about 120 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed this galaxy in visible and near-infrared light. The color assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of this data is near-infrared light, invisible to the eye, and long exposures reveal far more than an eye could.

explore: Type Ia supernovae come from exploding white dwarfs that have companion stars, and they always reach the same peak brightness, 5 billion times that of the Sun. Comparing that known true brightness with how bright one appears gives astronomers a way to measure distances across the universe.
alt: A face-on spiral galaxy with symmetrical, tightly wound arms curling from a pale yellow ring around a bright central bar and bulge.
